// Group WhatsApp turns without putting phone numbers in session identifiers.
export function conversationSessionId(threadId: string): string {
  return createHash("sha256").update(threadId).digest("hex");
}

export async function traceRequest<T>(
  channel: "whatsapp" | "cli",
  sessionId: string,
  run: () => Promise<T>,
  input?: unknown,
): Promise<T> {
  await telemetryReady;
  return trace({
    name: `${channel}.request`,
    kind: "WORKFLOW",
    sessionId,
    sessionEntryPoint: channel,
    input,
    attributes: { "app.channel": channel },
  }, async (activeSpan) => {
    console.info("Neatlogs trace started", { channel, traceId: activeSpan.spanContext().traceId, sessionId });
    log("Request started", { channel });
    try {
      const result = await run();
      log("Request completed", { channel });
      return result;
    } catch (error) {
      log("Request failed", { channel, level: "error", error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error) });
      throw error;
    }
  });
}

Yes, you're right about neatlogs, with one caveat. And yes, WhatsApp is limiting for this kind of product. I checked `src/telemetry.ts`, `package.json` and the `.entire/` folder so this matches your setup.

## 1. Neatlogs only works when it's inside the program

Your app calls `init()` from the `neatlogs` package and wraps each request in `trace()` (`src/telemetry.ts`). That means:
- It only sees code that runs inside your Node process. Anything outside it (another service, a Python script, an LLM call made somewhere else) is not traced unless that code also loads the SDK.
- If the process crashes before traces are sent, you can lose them.
- You can't attach it to an agent that's already running without changing its code.

**The caveat:** neatlogs looks like it's built on OpenTelemetry (your code uses `kind`, `spanContext().traceId` and an `endpoint` option). If their backend accepts the standard OpenTelemetry (OTLP) format, then any instrumented service could send traces to it without the neatlogs SDK. Putting an LLM proxy in front of your model calls could also capture traffic without touching the agent code. I haven't confirmed whether neatlogs supports either one, so check their docs before you count on it.

**Entire is the opposite.** It works outside your program, through git and agent hooks (your `.entire/` folder and the Codex/Antigravity hooks commit). It records how the code was built by coding agents. Neatlogs records how the product behaves while running. They work well together:
- **Entire** = build-time history
- **Neatlogs** = runtime traces

## 2. Is WhatsApp limiting? Yes, for a CFO-style agent

| Limitation | Why it hurts you |
|---|---|
| Text-only, about 4096 characters per message, no tables or charts | Financial answers need tables and charts |
| Business API 24-hour window, and pre-approved templates to start a chat | The agent can't freely send alerts on its own |
| At most 3 buttons or 10 list items per message | Hard to approve, drill down or edit |
| You can't link a reply to its trace or show "why the agent said this" | You lose most of what neatlogs gives you |
| Message delivery and media setup go through Meta (Business API) | Harder to iterate and demo |

## 3. What I'd recommend: use several interfaces with one agent behind them

1. **Main interface: a web app** (Next.js with the `ai-elements` and `shadcn` skills you already have). It can stream chat, show tables and charts and display tool calls, with a "view trace" link to neatlogs on each answer. This is where your observability story is visible. Very good for a hackathon demo.
2. **WhatsApp as the quick-access channel**: short questions, alerts and approvals ("Approve ₹40k spend? Yes/No"), with a link to the web app for details. Keep what you've built for this.
3. **Optionally Slack or Telegram**: richer formatting and buttons, no 24-hour rule. Your `chat` SDK supports them through adapters, so adding one is mostly config.
4. **Optionally an MCP server**: lets Claude Code or Codex query the CFO agent directly. This fits nicely with Entire, which records those sessions.

Because the agent code (`src/mastra`) is shared, every interface goes through the same `traceRequest(channel, …)`. Each new interface only needs a new `channel` value (`"web"`, `"slack"`) in that function's type.

I can scope the web interface as a first small sprint (chat page plus trace links) if you want to build it.

## What it is

An agent platform that runs inside your own infrastructure. Docker Compose brings up every part of it, the data sits in your PostgreSQL, and the model is yours to choose: no model ships in the box, and an administrator supplies the credential, which is encrypted at rest and never logged.

A deployment starts with two coworkers, and they are configuration rather than code: **General Assistant** for everyday work and **Knowledge** for company questions. A **Risk Analyst** joins them once its endpoint is configured, and ten more wait in `examples/fintech/catalog/`, each doing one job — reading an expense claim against the policy as written, turning a meeting note into the follow-ups actually in it, drafting release notes from what shipped, triaging a ticket, answering a new starter from the handbook, writing a brief that names what it could not find, writing up an interview, handing an on-call shift over, assembling what is known before a renewal, and grouping customer feedback into themes it can cite. Copy one into `examples/fintech/agents/` to add it, write your own there or in `agents.yaml`, or make one from `/agents` in the UI.

Anything a Bot does to a computer, a file, an MCP server or a component goes through one gateway that decides and records it. That is the difference between an agent that can use your tools and an agent you can let near them.

More at copilotkit.ai/openbot.

## Built on AG-UI

A Bot is any endpoint speaking AG-UI, the open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so OpenBot is not tied to a framework and neither are you. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or written by hand all arrive the same way, and the governance rides the protocol rather than the framework.



## Requirements

* Docker, for PostgreSQL and the shipped Bots.
* Bun 1.3+, for the app and API server.
* A CopilotKit Intelligence project and license. A free plan is available, and Intelligence can be self-hosted.
* A model key. The proof-of-concept Bot uses OpenAI; the LangGraph Bot can use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google.

## Quick start

> **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Paste `prompt.txt` into it first. It carries the
> same steps as below plus the things that are easy to get wrong: which of the blank keys in
> `.env.example` are actually yours to fill (the CopilotKit key and a model key), which the start
> script fills for you, and what each start-up refusal means. Every claim in it is checked against
> this repository.

1. Create `.env`:

   ```
   cp .env.example .env
   bun install
   ```
2. Connect a fresh managed Intelligence project:

   ```
   npx --yes copilotkit@latest login
   npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select
   bun scripts/setup-learning.ts
   ```

   The helper provisions the selected project's runtime key, creates or reuses its
   `openbot` Learning container, then writes both settings to `.env`. It preserves
   custom container assignments and refuses to replace an existing OpenBot key.
   For fresh self-hosted setup, set `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL` to that deployment's
   HTTPS API origin (or `http://localhost` for a local one) and run the helper
   without the two `npx` commands. It opens an isolated Chrome or Edge window for
   your usual sign-in and project choice; install either browser first. It writes
   the API URL, the key and the container, not `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL`, so
   set that one to the same deployment yourself. Existing key-only setups can assign a container
   through Admin → Automatic Learning.
   Managed Intelligence needs no separate licence token.
3. Fill the remaining required values:

   * `OPENAI_API_KEY`

   Keep the managed Intelligence URLs from `.env.example` unless you run Intelligence yourself. The example `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is public and fine locally; generate your own with:

   ```
   openssl rand -base64 32
   ```
4. Run:

   ```
   bash scripts/start.sh
   ```
5. Open http://localhost:3010.

`scripts/start.sh` starts Docker services, applies migrations, starts the API server on port 3001, starts the routine worker, starts the app on port 3010, and checks that the services answer their own health routes before printing next steps.

`scripts/stop.sh` takes the same things down, including each Bot's computer, which compose does not own; `--keep-computers` leaves the computers running. Nothing is deleted: the database, the Bots' files and their browser profiles are volumes.

### Intelligence on your own machine

To try Intelligence on one Mac instead of the managed service, follow
Evaluate Intelligence locally. The free
Developer plan qualifies. The local licence lasts 30 days and
`npx copilotkit@latest local renew` renews it as often as you need, while your account is in good

not a production installation. Run its
`npx copilotkit@latest local connect` from the OpenBot root, where `.env` is.

That command writes `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL`, `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL` and

## Deploy it

One image carries the app, the API, the browser the Bots drive, and optionally PostgreSQL. Same
`.env`, no Kubernetes.

```
# The published image. Nothing to clone and nothing to build.
docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \
  -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql \
  ghcr.io/copilotkit/openbot:latest

# Or the tree you have in front of you.
docker build -t openbot .
docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \
  -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql openbot
```

Everything is on 3001 here, the app included, rather than the 3010 the clone uses. `latest` is the
most recent release and a version tag such as `:v0.0.9` pins one.

Leave `EMBEDDED_POSTGRES` off and set `DATABASE_URL` to point at a database you already run.

## The stack they share

| Layer | rakazo (`apps/web`) | paperclip (`ui/`) |

| Terminal view | xterm | xterm |
| Chat | Their own `@rakazo/chat-ui` | **`@assistant-ui/react`**, which has an official Mastra integration |
| Talks to the backend via | **oRPC** typed calls (`@rakazo/contracts`) to a Hono API | Paperclip server REST API + TanStack Query |
| Backend | Hono, Postgres/Prisma, Better Auth | Node server, Postgres |
| License | Apache-2.0 (keep the license and attribution) | MIT |

Neither uses Next.js, and both match your Mastra (Hono) server well.

## Taking only the UI from each

**rakazo: best if you want the Grok Bot look.**
- Its README says that once it's running "it is just chat, like Grok Bot": you create bots and manage them from chat.
- Its component package `@rakazo/ui-web` is clean and easy to copy into our project.
- What we'd change: replace the typed calls in `@rakazo/contracts` with calls to your agents, either Mastra's client or AI SDK `useChat` with `@mastra/ai-sdk`.
- Effort: medium. The layout and components copy over; the data hooks get rewritten.

**paperclip: best if you want a "company of agents" dashboard.**
- The UI is shaped like a task manager and org chart. Its agent chat is still marked experimental.
- Its chat uses assistant-ui, which can connect straight to Mastra.
- Lifting only the UI is harder because it imports Paperclip's own agent adapters and server API.
- The easier route is to run Paperclip as a whole and add your Mastra agents through its HTTP adapter, but then it isn't really "just the UI".
- It also uses `@chat-adapter/*`, the same Chat SDK your WhatsApp bot uses.

Yes, I'd collapse it into a single app: one command, one port, one ngrok URL. But I'd keep `web/` as its own folder with its own `package.json`. Merging the code itself isn't worth it.

**Collapse these:**
- **Production, one process:** `src/server.ts` serves the built `web/dist` files plus `/api/*` and the WhatsApp webhook, all on :3000. Your existing ngrok tunnel then serves the UI, the API and WhatsApp from one domain, so no CORS setup and no second tunnel.

- **Root scripts:** add `npm run web:build` and have `npm run bot` handle both modes.

**Keep separate:**
- **`web/package.json` and tsconfig.** Browser code needs browser type definitions, React, Tailwind and Vite. Your server needs Node types and Mastra. Merging them into one tsconfig makes the type settings messy, and `mastra build` could end up trying to bundle React code. Separate folders keep each side lean.

content.text:
Your error comes from the Market Researcher agent, not the UI. One Crustdata tool returns so much raw data that the model ran out of room. DeepSeek's limit is 1,048,576 tokens, and that one Zepto request needed about 1.33M, so the run failed partway through.

## Why it happens (`src/mastra/tools/crustdata.ts`)
- **`crustdataCompanyEnrich`** (line 59) passes back the whole `company_data` object for up to 2 matches. The default sections include `people`, `competitors`, `headcount` and `funding`. For a company like Zepto that means thousands of people records and full headcount history, megabytes of JSON. That goes into the model's context on every following step.
- **`crustdataCompanySearch`** (line 86) returns `data.companies` without trimming it. If Crustdata ignores the `fields` list, each row is a full profile.
- The agent then called 5 tools in one turn (3, then 2). Each call stacked more of that data into the context until it overflowed.
- **Side effects:**
  - neatlogs drops the trace (`oversized span rejected`, span over 4 MB), so you can't see these runs.
  - The browser re-sends every past tool output with each new message. A large chat would soon hit the server's 1 MB request limit and get a 413 error even after the model issue is fixed.

## What's left to fix, by priority
| # | Fix | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Shrink tool outputs.** Keep only the fields the agent needs: cap `people` at about 10 key people, `competitors` at about 10, headcount at latest plus 12-month growth, recent funding rounds only, text fields shortened. Trim search rows to the 6 requested fields. Add a hard size cap, e.g. about 8–12k tokens per tool result. | `crustdata.ts` |

Yes, both have native solutions, and the docs confirm they fit together. (3) also gives us saved history (S8) at the same time.

## (2) Context limiter: Mastra's built-in processors
From `@mastra/core/processors` (moved there in Mastra v1):
- **`ToolCallFilter`** removes **old tool calls and results from what the model sees**, while keeping them in memory and in the UI. That's the exact cause of your Zepto problem.
- **`TokenLimiterProcessor`** drops the oldest non-system messages once a token budget is reached, so the model's limit can't be hit.

These get added to each agent's config. No custom code.

## (3) Stop re-sending history: Mastra Memory + AI SDK's "send only the last message"
- **Mastra docs:** "`chatRoute()` and `handleChatStream()` already work with memory. Configure the client to send only the new message and include the thread and resource identifiers." Memory loads past messages from storage before each model call and saves new ones afterwards.
- **AI SDK docs** (*Chatbot Message Persistence*): use the transport's built-in `prepareSendMessagesRequest` option to send only the last message plus the chat id.
- **What this needs:**
  - A storage adapter, `@mastra/libsql`: a local SQLite file, so no server to run.
  - `Memory` attached to the agents, configured with the processors above.
  - The server passing `memory: { thread: chatId, resource: … }` to `handleChatStream`. The server picks the resource id, so the browser can't read other users' chats.
  - On page load, the UI fetching the thread's saved messages (Mastra's memory API plus `toAISdkV5Messages`) instead of starting empty.

**What you get:** the browser sends only the new message, tool outputs stay on the server, history survives reloads (S8 done too), and the "in-memory store" warning goes away.

**The one judgment call:** a chat id per agent. I'd use the agent key plus a random id stored in the browser, and "New chat" creates a new one. Each "thread" (the stored conversation) also needs a "resource" (the owner the threads are grouped under). With no login yet, a fixed `web-user` resource is fine for now.

1. Add `@mastra/libsql` and Memory with `ToolCallFilter` and `TokenLimiterProcessor` on the 3 agents. Versions and APIs checked against the docs, not memory.
2. Server: pass `memory { thread, resource }` and add `GET /api/chat/:agentId/history`.
3. Web: `prepareSendMessagesRequest` sends only the last message, history loads on start, "New chat" starts a new thread.
4. Test: run the Zepto search twice in one chat, check each request carries only the new message, reload the page and confirm history is still there, and confirm WhatsApp and the CLI still work.
